client: I've been really anxious about this weekend because my partner wants me to meet their friends for the first time, and I just can't stop thinking about it. I keep imagining all these scenarios where they don't like me or think I'm not good enough for my partner. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it will change how I feel, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a quiet but persistent worry about this weekend — your voice has a kind of soft, tentative quality that tells me this feels both stressful and a little vulnerable to even talk about. Those "what if they don't like me" thoughts are really common before high-stakes social moments, and they tend to feel very convincing even when they're not based on evidence. I'm really glad you gave this a shot, because one thing we can work on together is gently examining whether those imagined scenarios reflect reality, or whether your mind might be filling in the blanks with fear rather than facts.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I mean... I hear what you're saying, but it's hard to just tell myself "oh, that's just fear, not facts" when the fear feels so real in the moment. Like, I've been to social gatherings before where I could just tell people weren't really interested in talking to me, so it's not like I'm making it up out of nowhere. It doesn't feel like my mind filling in blanks — it feels like I'm just being realistic about how these things usually go for me.
therapist: You're speaking quickly and there's a real tension in your voice — it sounds like this isn't just abstract worry, it genuinely stings, and you're pushing back a little because you don't want what you're feeling to be dismissed. You're absolutely right that past experiences where you felt overlooked are real and valid — I'm not trying to erase those. What I'd gently invite you to explore is whether those past moments are the *whole* story about how you come across to people, or whether they've become the loudest evidence your mind reaches for when you're feeling vulnerable.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, I mean... you're probably right that I'm pushing back a bit. It's just that when you say "maybe it's not the whole story," part of me wants to believe that, but then I think about all the times I've tried to connect with people and it just... fizzled out, and I'm left feeling like maybe the common denominator really is me. It's hard to trust that my mind is just cherry-picking the bad stuff when the bad stuff feels so consistent.
therapist: The way you're speaking — fast, with a kind of strained pitch — tells me this thought that "the common denominator is me" carries a lot of weight, even if you're saying it quietly. That belief is worth slowing down with, because our minds are remarkably good at building a consistent-feeling case against ourselves by cataloguing every fizzled connection while quietly skipping over the moments where things *did* click. I'd gently ask — are there any times, even small ones, where you felt genuinely received by someone, and if so, what does your mind do with those memories when this story starts to take over?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean... yeah, there are a few times. My friend Dara used to make me feel really seen — like she'd remember small things I said weeks later and bring them up. But when I think about that now, my brain kind of just... files it under "well, that ended too, didn't it," and uses it as more evidence against me rather than letting it actually count for anything good.
therapist: The softness in your voice as you talked about Dara tells me that memory still holds something tender and meaningful — and what you just described is actually a really important pattern to notice: your mind isn't ignoring the good evidence, it's *reframing* it as more proof of loss rather than letting it stand as proof of connection. Dara genuinely saw you, remembered you, valued you — and that happened because of *you*, not in spite of you, and the friendship ending doesn't retroactively erase what was real between you. What might it feel like to let that memory count as evidence that you *are* someone worth knowing, even just for a moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, I really do. But it's hard not to think that maybe Dara just... saw something in me that wasn't really there, or that I was just good at performing closeness for a while before she eventually figured out the truth. And even if I try to let that memory count as evidence, it feels like it's sitting on one side of a scale that's completely weighed down by everything that came after.
therapist: There's something in your voice — a kind of strained, high quality — that tells me this idea that you were "performing" and Dara eventually found out the truth is one that cuts really deep, even as you're saying it somewhat quietly. What you're describing has a name in CBT — it's called the "impostor" pattern, where the mind takes genuine connection and reframes it as accidental or fraudulent, so that *you* never get to be the reason anything good happened. I want to gently sit with this question together: if Dara — someone who remembered the small things, who *paid attention* — was being deceived by a performance, what would that say about her perceptiveness, and does that actually match who she sounds like she was?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That's... actually a hard question to dodge, because you're right that Dara wasn't someone you could fool easily. She picked up on things I didn't even say out loud, little shifts in my mood, things I'd half-mentioned weeks before. But I think what my brain keeps coming back to is — maybe she saw what she wanted to see, and I just happened to fit the shape of it, you know?
therapist: Your voice has a kind of breathless, high quality right now — like part of you can see the corner you've talked yourself into, but your mind is working very fast to find another exit. Notice what just happened though: you acknowledged that Dara was perceptive, that she couldn't easily be fooled, and then almost in the same breath your mind generated a brand new explanation to make sure you still don't get credit. That's not reasoning — that's a belief protecting itself, and it's worth asking: at what point does the evidence actually get to land?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and honestly it kind of stops me for a second because... yeah, I can feel that happening in real time, like my brain is already lining up the next argument even as I'm sitting here. It's uncomfortable to notice that, like catching yourself doing something you didn't realize you were doing. But I guess I'm scared that if I let the evidence "land," as you put it, I'll have to actually believe something different about myself, and I don't know if I'm ready for that.
therapist: The way you're speaking — fast, with a kind of high, strained quality — tells me that what you just said took real courage, and that noticing this pattern in real time is both uncomfortable and genuinely significant. What you're describing is actually the heart of the work: that changing a belief isn't just an intellectual exercise, it means letting go of a story about yourself that, however painful, has felt *certain* — and certainty, even painful certainty, can feel safer than the unknown. You don't have to be ready all at once — just being willing to sit with "maybe I'm wrong about myself" for a moment, like you're doing right now, is already something different.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually gets it, like logically I understand that holding onto "I'm someone who drives people away" is its own kind of comfort because at least I know what to expect. But sitting with "maybe I'm wrong" feels almost more terrifying than just accepting the loneliness, because if I'm wrong, then what's been keeping me isolated all this time was... me, and I don't know what to do with that. It's like opening a door I'm not sure I want to walk through.
therapist: The softness in your voice right now, even as you're speaking quickly, tells me this landed somewhere very deep and tender — and what you just named is one of the most honest and courageous things a person can say in this kind of work. You're right that realizing the barrier was inside you all along can feel like grief rather than relief, because it means mourning time and connection that didn't have to be lost. But I want you to hold this gently: that realization isn't a verdict on who you *are* — it's actually the first moment where the door to something different becomes real, and you're already standing in front of it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, I really do. But standing in front of a door doesn't mean I know how to open it, or that anyone's going to be on the other side waiting when I finally do. The loneliness has been there so long that I'm not even sure I'd know what to do with real connection if it actually showed up.
therapist: Your voice is soft and high right now, almost like you're speaking from somewhere very quiet and tired — and what you're describing, that loneliness becoming so familiar it feels like the only thing you know how to hold, is one of the most human and heartbreaking things there is. But I want to gently offer this: not knowing what to do with connection isn't the same as being incapable of it — it just means it would feel new, and new things feel uncertain, not impossible. And for what it's worth, the way you've shown up in this conversation today — honest, reflective, willing to sit with hard things — that *is* you practicing connection, right now, in real time.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but another part of me is thinking... this is different, talking to you. You're supposed to listen, that's the whole point of being here, so it doesn't really count the same way as trying to connect with someone out in the real world. I guess I'm just not sure that being able to do this here means I can actually do it out there, where people aren't paid to be patient with me.
therapist: The tightness and speed in your voice tells me this thought — that connection here "doesn't count" — isn't just a logical argument, it's a way of protecting yourself from hoping too much. And I want to name what I notice: this is the same pattern we've been watching all session, where your mind takes something real and finds a reason it doesn't get to count as evidence. What you've shown here today — the honesty, the willingness to be vulnerable, the courage to sit with uncomfortable things — those aren't skills you borrowed from me, they're yours, and they'll still belong to you on Saturday.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
